# Introduction to R {#sec-intro-r}

## Prerequisites

Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass this
chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the chapter in
@sec-quiz-answers-intro-r.

1. What is the difference between `c(1, 'a')` and `list(1, 'a')`?
2. In the expression `df[df$x > 0, ]`, what kind of R object is
   `df$x > 0`, and what rule does R use to combine it with the
   comma to select rows?
3. Predict the output of `x <- 1:5; x[-1]`, `x[c(TRUE, FALSE)]`,
   and `x[[1]]`. Which of these produces something that is *not*
   a numeric vector of length less than 5?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Install R and RStudio and configure a sensible working
  environment.
- Read the R documentation system (`?`, `??`, `help()`).
- Distinguish between atomic vectors, lists, and the major data
  structures built on them.
- Subset and mutate data with base R and with `dplyr`.
- Write vectorized expressions and explain why they outperform
  equivalent `for` loops.

## Orientation

R is the *lingua franca* of statistical computing in academic
biostatistics. It is not the fastest language, nor the most
elegant. It does, however, have by far the richest library of
statistical methods. It also has the largest community of
statisticians reading, writing, and reviewing code. Our aim in
this chapter is to make the reader fluent enough in R to read
the rest of the book.

We begin with the decisions that remain with the statistician,
and then turn to installation and the organization of an R
session. We then cover atomic vectors and coercion,
subsetting, and vectorization. The chapter closes with the
essentials of the tidyverse and a set of prompts for working
with an LLM.

## The statistician's contribution {#sec-intro-r-human}

Large language models can produce passable R code for almost
any introductory task. We shall see, however, that three
decisions still require the judgment of the statistician.

**1. Type discipline.** R coerces silently between types in
ways that can hide errors. `c(1, '2')` becomes
`c('1', '2')` (character); `TRUE + 1` becomes `2` (double).
An LLM will happily accept whatever types flow through its
generated code. It is therefore necessary for you to decide,
before any computation runs, which types the data *should*
carry. Where it matters, you should assert them with
`stopifnot(is.numeric(x))`.

**2. Base R vs tidyverse framing.** The same transformation
can be expressed in base R and in `dplyr`. An LLM will lean
toward whichever style dominated its training data, which is
usually `dplyr` for interactive work. The tradeoffs in
performance, dependencies, and readability belong to you, and
the needs of the project should settle them.

**3. Edge cases in statistical data.** R's built-in functions
handle `NA`, `NaN`, `Inf`, zero-length vectors, and
length-mismatched vectors in different ways. The defaults
are usually right for general-purpose data. Unfortunately,
they are often wrong for biomedical data, where missingness is
informative. An LLM will not check whether your data have the
edge cases that would break its generated code, and so that
check falls to you.

## Installing R and RStudio

R is a free and open-source implementation of the S
programming language. The base R installer may be downloaded
from the Comprehensive R Archive Network
([CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/)). Posit's RStudio
Desktop, a free integrated development environment, is
available at <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>.
Install R first, then RStudio.

On macOS, the `rig` command-line tool
(<https://github.com/r-lib/rig>) lets you install and switch
between R versions cleanly:

```sh
brew install --cask rig
rig add release        # installs the current stable R
rig default release
```

We then verify the installation:

```sh
R --version
# R version 4.5.3 (2026-02-28) -- 'Single Candle'
```

When RStudio is launched, its default four-pane layout
provides a script editor, a console, an environment
inspector, and a files/plots/help browser.

## The R console, scripts, and projects

An R session is anchored to a working directory and a set of
loaded packages. Two conventions make sessions reproducible.

**Use RStudio projects.** A `.Rproj` file tells RStudio that
the enclosing directory is a project. Opening the file sets
the working directory automatically and isolates the session
from the rest of your filesystem. We recommend that you always
work inside a project, never from a stray session rooted in
`~/`.

**Prefer scripts over the console.** The console is for quick
exploration, and scripts are for work that must be
reproducible. A script is a `.R` or `.qmd` file that you can
rerun from top to bottom to obtain the same result. Analyses
that live only in the console history are lost when the
session ends.

The `.Rprofile` file in a project runs automatically when you
open a session. It is the natural place to set session-wide
options, such as the CRAN mirror or the preferred number of
significant digits. The `renv` package extends this pattern to
pin package versions. Package and environment management is
covered in detail in the practicum companion volume.

## Atomic vectors and coercion

Everything in R is built from vectors. Even a single number
like `5` is a vector of length 1.

R has six atomic types: `logical`, `integer`, `double`,
`character`, `complex`, and `raw`. The last two are rarely
used in statistical work. All elements of an atomic vector
share a type. When we combine mixed types, R
silently coerces them to the most general type in the chain
`logical → integer → double → character`.

```{.r}
c(TRUE, 1L)         # -> integer: 1, 1
c(TRUE, 1L, 2.5)    # -> double:  1.0, 1.0, 2.5
c(TRUE, 1L, 'x')    # -> character: 'TRUE', '1', 'x'
```

Silent coercion is a common source of bugs. To illustrate,
`sum(c(1, 2, NA))` returns `NA`, not `3`. Similarly,
`mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))` returns `0.667` because the
logicals coerce to `c(1, 0, 1)`. That result is numerically
correct and often useful, but it can surprise readers.

**Lists** differ from atomic vectors in that their elements
can each carry a different type:

```{.r}
list(1, 'a', TRUE)    # length-3 list, three distinct types
```

Operations that work on atomic vectors often do not work on
lists. When iterating over list elements, the appropriate
tools are `lapply()`, `sapply()`, or `purrr::map_*()`
(@sec-functional).

**Special values:**

- `NA` is missing data. Most operations involving `NA` return
  `NA`.
- `NULL` is the absence of an object. Assigning `NULL` to a
  list element removes it.
- `NaN` is 'not a number' (for example, `0/0`).
- `Inf` and `-Inf` are the signed infinities (for example,
  `1/0`).

::: {.callout-tip collapse='true'}
## Check your understanding

**Q:** What does `c(1, 'a')` return, and why?

**A:** The character vector `c('1', 'a')`. R cannot store
`1` and `'a'` in the same atomic vector, so it coerces both
to the most general type (character). To keep the original
types, use `list(1, 'a')`.
:::

## Subsetting: `[`, `[[`, and `$`

R offers three subsetting operators and four kinds of
indices. Confusion between them is the most common source of
errors in a first R course.

**The three operators.**

- `[` returns a subset of the same type as the original. For
  an atomic vector it returns a vector; for a list it returns
  a list; for a data frame it returns a data frame.
- `[[` returns a single element, stripping the container.
  From a list, `[[` gives you the element itself (which might
  be any type); from an atomic vector, `[[` returns a length-1
  atomic of the same type.
- `$name` is shorthand for `[['name']]` on a list or data
  frame.

**The four index types.**

```{.r}
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

x[2]              # positive integer: 20
x[c(1, 3, 5)]     # vector of positive integers: 10, 30, 50
x[-1]             # negative integer: drop element 1 -> 20, 30, 40, 50
x[x > 25]         # logical: 30, 40, 50
x[c('a', 'b')]    # character: works only if x has names
```

For data frames, `[row, col]` applies the subsetting rules
along both dimensions. The expression `df[df$x > 0, ]` uses a
logical row index (`df$x > 0`) to keep the rows where `x` is
positive. The missing column index keeps all columns.

```{.r}
df <- data.frame(
  id  = 1:5,
  x   = c(3, -1, 5, 0, 8),
  grp = c('a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a')
)

df[df$x > 0, ]        # rows where x is positive
df[df$grp == 'a', ]   # rows in group 'a'
df[, c('id', 'x')]    # two columns, all rows
```

We note that a logical index built from a column containing
`NA` produces `NA` rows rather than dropping those rows, a
behavior that surprises many users. If you want the `NA` rows
dropped, use `which()` or `subset()`.

## Vectorization

Vectorization means applying an operation to every element of
a vector at once, without an explicit loop. It is the central
design principle of R, and nearly every built-in function is
vectorized.

```{.r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
x + 10                # 11 12 13 14 15, elementwise
x^2                   # 1 4 9 16 25
sqrt(x)               # 1.00 1.41 1.73 2.00 2.24
```

When two vectors of different lengths combine, R recycles the
shorter vector to match the longer:

```{.r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)    # 11 22 13 24  (recycled)
```

On the one hand, recycling without warning is convenient for
scalar + vector arithmetic. On the other, it is dangerous when
lengths mismatch by accident. R warns if the longer length is
not a multiple of the shorter, but not otherwise.

**Loop vs vectorized.** The following benchmark compares the
two on the same computation:

```{.r}
library(bench)

vectorised_zscore <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)

loop_zscore <- function(x) {
  z <- numeric(length(x))
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sd(x)
  for (i in seq_along(x)) z[i] <- (x[i] - m) / s
  z
}

bench::mark(
  vectorised = vectorised_zscore(iris$Sepal.Length),
  loop       = loop_zscore(iris$Sepal.Length),
  iterations = 100
)
```

The vectorized version is faster because the elementwise
arithmetic happens in compiled C code, not in R's
interpreter. The size of the gap depends on the R version, the
hardware, and the length of the vector. On one recent laptop
running R 4.6, the vectorized version was roughly twice as
fast for the 150 values of `iris$Sepal.Length`. For a vector
of length 1 million it was roughly ten times as fast. R's
byte-code compiler has narrowed the gap considerably for
simple loops of this kind.

::: {.callout-tip collapse='true'}
## Check your understanding

**Q:** Why is vectorized R code faster than an equivalent
`for` loop that does the same arithmetic?

**A:** The vectorized operation hands the whole vector to a
compiled C routine, which runs the loop internally at native
speed. An R-level `for` loop invokes the R interpreter once
per element, and the interpreter overhead dominates the
actual arithmetic for simple operations.
:::

Not every algorithm vectorizes. Sequential updates (MCMC
chains, sequential hypothesis tests, change-point detection)
require each step to depend on the previous one. Such updates
cannot be written as single elementwise expressions. For these
cases, `Rcpp` (@sec-r-internals) lets us write a C++ loop that
R calls as a single function.

## Tidyverse essentials

The tidyverse is a coordinated set of packages (`dplyr`,
`tidyr`, `ggplot2`, `purrr`, and others) that share a common
grammar for data manipulation and visualization. The `dplyr`
package provides six core verbs and a pipe operator that
chains them.

The native R pipe `|>` (introduced in R 4.1, 2021) passes its
left-hand side as the first argument to the right-hand side:

```{.r}
x |> mean()          # same as mean(x)
x |> round(digits = 2)  # same as round(x, digits = 2)
```

Earlier tidyverse code uses the magrittr pipe `%>%`. The two
are similar, and this book uses the native pipe exclusively.

The six `dplyr` verbs apply to data frames:

| Verb | Action |
|---|---|
| `filter(df, condition)` | Keep rows where condition is TRUE |
| `select(df, cols)`      | Keep or drop columns |
| `mutate(df, new = ...)` | Add or modify columns |
| `summarise(df, ...)`    | Reduce to a single row (or one per group) |
| `arrange(df, col)`      | Sort rows |
| `group_by(df, col)`     | Group for later verbs |

To illustrate, consider a typical pipeline:

```{.r}
library(dplyr)

ChickWeight |>
  filter(Time <= 14) |>
  group_by(Diet, Time) |>
  summarise(
    mean_weight = mean(weight),
    n           = n(),
    .groups     = 'drop'
  ) |>
  arrange(Diet, Time)
```

The pipe reads from top to bottom like an analysis plan. We
start with `ChickWeight`, keep the first 14 days, group by diet
and day, summarize, and sort. The same computation in base R
would fragment into intermediate variables and nested function
calls. The pipe, by contrast, keeps the data flow visible.

::: {.callout-tip collapse='true'}
## Check your understanding

**Q:** What does `df |> group_by(x) |> summarise(m = mean(y))`
return that `summarise(df, m = mean(y))` does not?

**A:** A data frame with one row per distinct level of `x`,
giving the mean of `y` within each group. Without
`group_by()`, the second form collapses the whole data frame
to a single row.
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM on R essentials

In @sec-intro-r-human we named three decisions that require
the judgment of the statistician. The prompts below exercise
each one. As elsewhere in the book, the reader should treat
the response of the LLM as a hypothesis to verify.

### Type coercion

**Prompt.** 'Read this CSV and compute the mean of the `dose`
column', then paste a CSV whose `dose` column mixes numeric
strings and the literal string `'NA'`.

**What to watch for.** `read.csv()` treats `'NA'` strings as
the missing sentinel by default, but `readr::read_csv()` has
different defaults depending on version. A `dose` column with
mixed content can silently come in as `character`. In that
case `mean()` on the character vector returns `NA` with a
warning. An LLM may also wrap the read in `as.numeric()`
without warning you that values that fail to parse become
`NA`.

**Verification.** Inspect `str(df$dose)` after the read.
Confirm that the type is `numeric` and that the count of `NA`
values matches the count of non-parseable source strings.

### Base R vs tidyverse

**Prompt.** 'Write R code to compute, for each level of a
grouping variable, the mean of another variable, dropping
missing values.'

**What to watch for.** An LLM will usually produce the
`dplyr` form (`group_by` + `summarise(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))`).
It may not ask whether the project uses the tidyverse at all.
Production R code in some settings runs on base R or
`data.table` and imports no tidyverse. Examples include
pharma, legacy packages, and FDA submissions via pharmaverse
internals.

**Verification.** Confirm the dependency policy of the project
before accepting the suggestion. If the tidyverse is
permitted, keep the code from the LLM. If not, ask for the base
R equivalent (`aggregate(y ~ group, data = df, FUN = mean)`)
or the `data.table` equivalent.

### Edge cases

**Prompt.** 'Write a function that computes the ratio of two
columns in a data frame.'

**What to watch for.** An LLM will typically write
`df$x / df$y` without handling the cases that make the ratio
undefined. These are zero denominators (which produce
`Inf`), negative denominators (which change the sign), `NA`
inputs (which propagate), and zero-row inputs (which return a
zero-length numeric). In a biomedical analysis each case
signals a real data phenomenon. A zero divisor may be a
structural zero, a missing value may be a censored
measurement, and so on.

**Verification.** Ask the LLM to list the inputs on which the
function would produce unexpected output. Then extend the
function to raise an error (with an explanatory message) in
cases that indicate broken data, instead of silently returning
`Inf` or `NaN`.

## Exercises

1. Write a function `summarise_numeric(df)` that takes a data
   frame and returns a data frame with one row per numeric column
   giving its mean, median, SD, and number of missing values.
   Do not use any package outside base R.
2. Repeat exercise 1 using `dplyr::summarise()` across all
   numeric columns. Compare the two implementations for
   readability and speed.
3. Explain, in at most three sentences, why
   `sum(c(1, 2, NA)) == NA` returns `NA` rather than `TRUE`.

- [@wickham2023r4ds], the canonical first book for R data analysis; the 2nd edition uses the native pipe throughout.
- [@wickham2019advr] Chapters 1-3, essential for reading other people's R code.
- [@grolemund2017r4ds], the 1st edition is still a readable slower-paced introduction to the tidyverse.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-intro-r}

1. `c(1, 'a')` coerces both elements to the most permissive
   atomic type, producing `c('1', 'a')` (character).
   `list(1, 'a')` preserves the types of each element
   because lists are not atomic.
2. `df$x > 0` is a logical vector of length `nrow(df)`. R
   applies logical subsetting along the first dimension of
   the data frame so that `df[df$x > 0, ]` keeps only the
   rows where the logical vector is `TRUE`. Rows where
   `df$x > 0` is `NA` are returned as rows of all `NA`.
3. `x[-1]` drops the first element and returns `2:5`.
   `x[c(TRUE, FALSE)]` recycles the logical vector to length
   5 and returns `c(1, 3, 5)`. `x[[1]]` returns the scalar
   `1`, which is still a length-1 numeric vector; the
   `[[ ]]` form is important conceptually (it strips
   list/vector structure) but on atomic vectors it behaves
   like `[ ]` with a single index. All three results are
   numeric vectors of length less than 5.
